chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from Abu al-Subah al-Kinanī, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the one who gives evidence of defamation (al-qadhf) after the punishment has been carried out against him, what is his repentance? He said: 'He lies about himself.' I said: 'Do you see if he lies about himself and repents, is his testimony accepted?' He said: 'Yes.'

key_terms.الْقَاذِفِ: The one who gives testimony of defamation (shahadat al-qadhf)
key_terms.يُقَامُ عَلَيْهِ الْحَدُّ: The punishment is carried out against him
key_terms.يُكْذِبُ نَفْسَهُ: He lies about himself (a specific legal form of retraction/admission)

ai.seo_question: What is the required repentance for a person who has undergone the hadd punishment for defamation to have their testimony accepted again?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that the repentance of the *qadhf*er (defamer) after receiving the hadd punishment requires him to 'lie about himself,' a juristic nuance often interpreted as admitting the truth of his previous accusation or retracting it in a manner that nullifies his prior testimony. This specific act of self-negation serves as the condition for the restoration of his legal credibility (*qabul al-shahadah*), highlighting the Shia emphasis on precise procedural repentance in family law. The hadith underscores the balance between maintaining the integrity of the judicial system and offering mercy to the repentant individual.
